---
title: "Lazy Evaluation"
---

# Lazy Evaluation

Adaptors build a description of work. Consumers run it, and they run only as far as they need.

## The concept

`readings.iter().map(f).filter(g)` is a struct that holds `readings`'s iterator, `f`, and `g`. No element is touched yet. The first call to `next` on that struct pulls one element from the inner iterator, runs `f`, and keeps pulling until `g` accepts one. `take(2)` stops after two accepted elements. `find` stops at the first match. The tail of the pipeline never runs.

## Recipe 8 — Confirming that adaptors are lazy

```rust
fn main() {
    use std::cell::Cell;

    let seen = Cell::new(0);
    let pipeline = [10, 20, 30, 40].into_iter().map(|n| {
        seen.set(seen.get() + 1);
        n / 10
    });

    assert_eq!(seen.get(), 0);

    let mut pipeline = pipeline;
    assert_eq!(pipeline.next(), Some(1));
    assert_eq!(seen.get(), 1);
    assert_eq!(pipeline.next(), Some(2));
    assert_eq!(seen.get(), 2);
}
```

One `next`, one call. The `30` and `40` are still untouched.

## Recipe 9 — Short-circuiting an expensive pipeline with take()

`take(n)` asks for `n` items and then returns `None`, even if the source is infinite or expensive.

```rust
fn main() {
    use std::cell::Cell;

    let parsed = Cell::new(0);
    let lines = [
        "sensor,1",
        "sensor,2",
        "sensor,3",
        "sensor,4",
        "sensor,5",
    ];

    let first_two: Vec<i32> = lines
        .into_iter()
        .map(|line| {
            parsed.set(parsed.get() + 1);
            line.split(',').nth(1).unwrap().parse().unwrap()
        })
        .take(2)
        .collect();

    assert_eq!(first_two, [1, 2]);
    assert_eq!(parsed.get(), 2);
}
```

Put `take` after the adaptor whose work you want to limit. `take(2).map(...)` also limits the `map`, because `map`'s `next` is only called twice. `map(...).take(2)` is the form to use when the limit is on the output, which is the same count here. If a later adaptor drops items (`filter`), `take` counts what comes out of that adaptor, so place it where the "how many" question is asked.

## Recipe 10 — Avoiding work with find() and position()

`find` returns the item. `position` returns the index. Both stop at the first hit.

```rust
fn main() {
    use std::cell::Cell;

    let checks = Cell::new(0);
    let readings = [3, 8, 11, 40, 41];

    let found = readings.iter().copied().find(|n| {
        checks.set(checks.get() + 1);
        *n > 10
    });
    assert_eq!(found, Some(11));
    assert_eq!(checks.get(), 3);

    let index = readings.iter().position(|n| *n > 10);
    assert_eq!(index, Some(2));
}
```

`position` does not need the side-effect counter. It walks `3`, `8`, then `11`, and stops. `rposition` starts from the other end when the iterator is `DoubleEndedIterator`.

There is no reason to `collect` a filtered `Vec` just to call `[0]` on it. `find` already is that search.

## Recipe 11 — Comparing lazy chains vs eager loops for clarity

Both programs keep readings at or above 20 and scale them by 10. The chain is one expression. The loop makes the push obvious.

```rust
fn main() {
    let readings = [18, 21, 19, 30, 12];

    let from_chain: Vec<_> = readings
        .iter()
        .copied()
        .filter(|n| *n >= 20)
        .map(|n| n * 10)
        .collect();

    let mut from_loop = Vec::new();
    for n in readings {
        if n >= 20 {
            from_loop.push(n * 10);
        }
    }

    assert_eq!(from_chain, [210, 300]);
    assert_eq!(from_loop, [210, 300]);
}
```

Prefer the chain when every step is a pure transformation of one element and the whole result is one collection. Prefer the loop when a step `break`s, updates two collections, or needs a comment longer than the line it would replace. Later recipes keep that line: a pipeline should stay readable as a sentence.
